causalMechanism.primaryVector: Pharmacological iatrogenic sequence: allopurinol is metabolized to oxypurinol, and in carriers of the HLA-B*58:01 allele the drug and its metabolite are presented as drug-specific antigens that activate cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes. The activated T cells release granulysin, perforin, and Fas-ligand, which trigger widespread keratinocyte apoptosis and detachment of the full-thickness epidermis — the mechanism of toxic epidermal necrolysis when detachment exceeds 30 percent of body surface area, and of Stevens-Johnson syndrome below that threshold. Mucosal surfaces, including the ocular surface and the oral, genital, and respiratory mucosae, are involved by the same cytotoxic process, and survivors are left with chronic morbidity: hypertrophic and dyspigmented scarring, sicca and ocular surface failure with symblepharon formation, oral and genital mucosal strictures, and recurrent mucosal episodes. Halevy et al. (PMID 17919772), a multinational case-control study, found that allopurinol was the single most common cause of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in Europe and Israel and identified risk factors for allopurinol-associated disease — the primary causal attribution evidence for this drug. Somkrua et al. (PMID 21906289) systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed the association between the HLA-B*5801 allele and allopurinol-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis and found a strong and significant association, concluding that allele screening may be considered in populations at risk. Gonçalo et al. (PMID 23600531) studied 25 Portuguese patients with allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions, including DRESS and Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis cases, and confirmed HLA-B*58:01 as a risk factor in a European population, extending the association beyond Han Chinese cohorts. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of the service-connected gout is itself service-connected because the allopurinol was prescribed for the service-connected condition; the compensable disability in most cases is the residual scarring, ocular surface disease, and mucosal sequelae rather than the acute hospitalization. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows a pre-existing skin disease such as psoriasis or another blistering disorder and the claim is that the drug reaction worsened a baseline dermatosis, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing disease and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: a prescription record identifying allopurinol with start and stop dates and the gout indication; acute-onset mucocutaneous disease documented by dermatology, ideally with histopathology or a registry-classified diagnosis of Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis with the estimated percentage of body surface area detached; the implicated-drug reasoning recorded in the acute admission; and documentation of the chronic sequelae that are actually being rated, such as scar extent, ocular surface findings, or mucosal stricture. Only then can an examiner state that the toxic epidermal necrolysis and its sequelae are at least as likely as not caused by the allopurinol prescribed for the service-connected gout — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include other high-risk culprits that are frequently co-prescribed — aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital), sulfonamide antibiotics and sulfasalazine, nevirapine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs of the oxicam class, and the newer checkpoint inhibitors — as well as DRESS syndrome with a different natural history, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, pemphigus vulgaris, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, and graft-versus-host disease. A specific causality caution must be disclosed: HLA-B*58:01 carriage is strongly associated with but is neither necessary nor sufficient for allopurinol hypersensitivity in every population, and the cited case-control data are population-level attributions, so a positive genotype or a negative genotype neither proves nor disproves causation in one veteran, and the acute drug-attribution reasoning recorded at the time of illness is the strongest single piece of evidence. No individual probability is asserted here. No intentional rechallenge, unsupervised discontinuation of a prescribed medication, or patient-specific prescribing recommendation is made. Rating discipline under § 4.14 and § 4.118(b): two skin conditions may be combined only where separate areas of skin are involved, and where the same skin supports ratings under DC 7827 and DC 7800, DC 7801 or DC 7804, only the higher single evaluation may be assigned for that area; ocular sequelae rated under § 4.79 are separate disabilities and must not be used twice.

Primary condition: Service-connected gout for which allopurinol was prescribed
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5017 (gout) — evaluated as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion of affected parts under the note to DCs 5013 through 5024
Secondary condition: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (drug-induced severe cutaneous adverse reaction with chronic cutaneous, ocular and mucosal sequelae) in a veteran receiving allopurinol for service-connected gout
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.118, DC 7827 (erythema multiforme; toxic epidermal necrolysis): 60 percent for recurrent mucosal, palmar, or plantar involvement impairing mastication, use of hands, or ambulation occurring four or more times over the past 12-month period despite ongoing immunosuppressive therapy; 30 percent for the corresponding recurrent pattern requiring intermittent systemic therapy; 10 percent for one to three such episodes in the past 12-month period or continuous systemic medication for control; alternatively rated as disfigurement of the head, face, or neck (DC 7800) or scars (DCs 7801, 7802, 7804, 7805) depending on the predominant disability. Ocular and other mucosal sequelae are separately rated in the affected system. Qualified-human rating review required
Original nexus theory: Medication Side Effect
